issue.body: The JSX transforms currently use double quotes when converting JSX nodes. This conflicts with the single quote rule. This is a test case (which currently fails) for this scenario.

body: This would only apply if you transform first and then lint the result. ESLint lints without transforming first, so I don't think any changes is necessary.
So maybe an issue with how esprima handles it? The test I provided fails with the single quote rule.
Can you try running ESLint from the command line on a file with that text and then paste the output you see into this issue? That would be very helpful in understanding what's going on.

Compare the JSX literal (loc and range removed):

``` js
{ type: 'Literal',
  value: 'Hello world',
  raw: 'Hello world',
  parent:
   { type: 'XJSElement',
     openingElement:
      { type: 'XJSOpeningElement',
        name: [Object],
        selfClosing: false,
        attributes: [],
        parent: [Circular] },
     closingElement:
      { type: 'XJSClosingElement',
        name: [Object],
        parent: [Circular] },
     children: [ [Circular] ],
     parent:
      { type: 'ExpressionStatement',
        expression: [Circular],
        parent: [Object] } } }
```

...with a normal `"use strict"` string literal (loc, range, parent removed):

``` js
{ type: 'Literal',
  value: 'use strict',
  raw: '"use strict"' }
```

The JSX literal has no quotes, which seems to me to be the correct behavior for the parser. As for the correct behavior here... perhaps don't warn if `parent.type  === "XJSElement"`?
Yeah, I think that's the right approach.

Upon further investigation, I'm not sure I like the parent idea anymore. From looking at the [JSX AST extensions](https://github.com/facebook/jsx/blob/master/AST.md), it'd be more than just `XJSElement` we'd have to worry about, and it would get even more complicated as one can embed normal JS in JSX, and we should still check the JS. Consider the following case: ``` jsx
Hello world
' ``` That AST looks like this: ``` { type: 'Program', body: [ { type: 'ExpressionStatement', expression: { type: 'XJSElement', openingElement: { type: 'XJSOpeningElement', name: { type: 'XJSIdentifier', name: 'div' }, selfClosing: false, attributes: [ { type: 'XJSAttribute', name: { type: 'XJSIdentifier', name: 'id' }, value: { type: 'XJSExpressionContainer', expression: { type: 'ConditionalExpression', test: { type: 'Identifier', name: 'test', typeAnnotation: undefined, optional: undefined }, consequent: { type: 'Literal', value: 'foo', raw: '"foo"' }, alternate: { type: 'Literal', value: 'bar', raw: '"bar"' } } } } ] }, closingElement: { type: 'XJSClosingElement', name: { type: 'XJSIdentifier', name: 'div' } }, children: [ { type: 'Literal', value: 'Hello world', raw: 'Hello world' } ] } } ] } ``` So, new idea: there's already a check in `lib/rules/quotes.js` for `typeof node.value === "string"`. Am I correct in my thinking that a Literal node will satisfy that test if and only if it was a JS string literal? If so, the unquoted string literal is unique to JSX, in which case the rule should ignore nodes whose raw value is unquoted, only warning when quotes are present and incorrect. Is that better?

I believe you're correct. Just to double check, @rreverser - it looks Esprima-FB represents strings embedded inside of JSX element as `Literal` nodes whose `raw` value is an unquoted string and `value` is a string. This is confusing ESLint because we typically do `typeof node.value === 'string'` to determine if it's a string literal or not. Is it correct to say that such a literal in JSX will be distinguishable from a regular JavaScript string literal in that `raw` won't begin or end with quotes? Or is there some better way of determining this? (It would be nice to be able to do so without needing `raw`, but we can make do if necessary.)

Yes, those are just regular `Literal` string nodes with unquoted `raw`, so it should do the trick.

However I probably missed smth in this discussion, so not sure what is the problem with `parent.type === 'XJSElement'`? It would be safer and easier-to-implement approach IMO.

Btw, one more thought - `raw` boundary quote test won't actually work in cases like the following: ``` html
"Yes, I'm quoted text on page, why not?"
```

I think the point was that there are a few elements rather than just `XJSElement` that would indicate it's inside of JSX content. 

Yeah, `raw` is generally unreliable. It would be nice if there was a way to differentiate between a JS literal and a literal inside of JSX. I suppose it's too late to change anything?

In the meantime, can we infer if the parent contains `XJS` then the literal is a JSX literal rather than an ecmascript literal?

> I think the point was that there are a few elements rather than just XJSElement that would indicate it's inside of JSX content. 

I'm not aware of such but `XJSElement` (at least those that could contain JSX string literal).

> In the meantime, can we infer if the parent contains XJS then the literal is a JSX literal rather than an ecmascript literal?

If you do so, then you also catch attribute values like `<div attr="quoted string" />` and `<div attr='quoted string' />` which would be mistake IMO.
https://github.com/eslint/eslint/blob/b9756ccb91de5deb3a11312d1f871438bb19b455/tests/lib/rules/quotes.js#L23 so you don't care about attributes to be quoted in the same way as other strings in code?
In my mind it's a completely different thing
